courseTitle: The ABA problem and tagged pointers
lessonTitle: How a stale CAS corrupts a lock-free stack
md: CAS checks *equality of value*, not *absence of change*. Any algorithm that reads a pointer, computes from what it points to, and then CASes on that pointer is wrong if the pointed-to node can be recycled in between.

courseTitle: Ablation studies: what each pipeline stage really adds
lessonTitle: Add-one-in vs leave-one-out on a fixed harness
md: Add-one-in measures a stage in isolation; leave-one-out measures its marginal value in the system you will ship. When the two disagree, the stages interact, and that disagreement is itself a finding worth reporting.

courseTitle: Broken access control and authorization design
lessonTitle: Case: First American Financial and 885 million documents (2019)
md: First American had two failures. The code failure was a missing object-level check. The process failure was treating a confirmed exposure of hundreds of millions of sensitive documents as low severity. Severity comes from what the bug exposes, not from how simple the bug is.

courseTitle: Broken access control and authorization design
lessonTitle: Testing authorization with role matrices, and detecting enumeration
md: Authorization is tested by asking the wrong user. For every endpoint, decide in advance what anonymous users, other users, other tenants and admins should get, write it down as a matrix, and make the build fail when reality differs.

courseTitle: Active Directory and Kerberos attacks
lessonTitle: Kerberoasting: service tickets that can be cracked offline
md: Kerberoasting works because any user may request any service ticket and the ticket is locked with a key derived from the service account's password. Remove human passwords from service accounts (gMSA), drop RC4, keep them unprivileged, and alert on RC4 4769s for user-owned SPNs.

courseTitle: Active Directory and Kerberos attacks
lessonTitle: When the DC itself has the bug: Zerologon, noPac, PrintNightmare
md: DC bugs turn a foothold into the domain in minutes, so DCs are patched first and fastest, run no extra services, and go to enforcement mode early. Zerologon, noPac and PrintNightmare each have specific events to watch.

courseTitle: Advanced malware analysis: maldocs, scripts, unpacking, anti-analysis
lessonTitle: Case: Follina (CVE-2022-30190), a document with no macro
md: Patches end a bug; detections outlive it. Word starting msdt.exe was abnormal before May 2022 and is still abnormal now, so the behaviour rule keeps catching the next abuse of a protocol handler.

courseTitle: Advanced malware analysis: maldocs, scripts, unpacking, anti-analysis
lessonTitle: Ransomware crypto mistakes: how Hive's files were decrypted
md: Never use one keystream twice. Reusing keystream material across files turns any file whose original you hold into a key for others. Sound designs encrypt each file with its own key from a proper cipher and protect the master secret with public-key encryption.

courseTitle: Advanced memory exploitation concepts: ROP, heap and kernel
lessonTitle: Exploit chains: renderer bug, sandbox escape, kernel bug
md: A full compromise of a hardened platform is a chain, usually renderer RCE plus sandbox escape plus kernel bug. Each extra wall forces another 0-day, and each stage is a separate chance to detect or break the attack.

courseTitle: Adversarial machine learning
lessonTitle: Stickers, turtles and malware: attacks outside the lab
md: Physical and problem-space attacks are real but constrained: they must survive transformations and keep the object working. Real attackers mostly use cheap manual tricks found by probing. Design so that one fooled model is not one fooled system.

courseTitle: Adversarial machine learning
lessonTitle: Training with differential privacy: DP-SGD and its price
md: An epsilon without its delta, its unit (one record, one user?) and its accountant is not a privacy claim. Ask what one 'record' means: if a user contributes 500 records, record-level DP says little about that user.

courseTitle: Adversary emulation, red teaming and purple teaming
lessonTitle: Detecting C2: beacons, egress and fingerprints
md: Regular is not the same as malicious. Software updaters, monitoring agents and chat clients poll on timers too. A beacon score is a hunting lead, ranked with rarity of the destination and the type of host, not an alert on its own. Allowlist known pollers by destination and process, and review the list, because an intruder can hide behind an allowlisted name.

courseTitle: Agent benchmarks: SWE-bench, tau-bench and reading the scores
lessonTitle: An agent benchmark is a task, an environment and a grader
md: An agent benchmark score is a property of **model + harness + environment + grader + metric**. Change any one and the number moves. Most of this course is about how each part shapes the score.

courseTitle: Agent harnesses: the loop, tools, context and control around an LLM
lessonTitle: A minimal harness: stop conditions, errors and budgets
md: Do not retry a tool blindly. Re-running a failed `git push` or a payment call can duplicate a side effect. Retry the model API transport freely, but report tool failures back to the model and let it decide, or make the tool itself idempotent, meaning running it twice has the same effect as running it once (for example, a payment call that carries a unique request key the server uses to ignore duplicates).

courseTitle: Agent long-term memory: what to store, update, retrieve and forget
lessonTitle: Consolidation and forgetting: reflection, decay and deletion
md: Deletion must follow lineage. Keep source pointers on every derived memory (Generative Agents already stores the cited records for each reflection) so that deleting a source can find and rewrite or delete every reflection, summary and merged fact that contains it. Also delete the embeddings and any copies in logs.

courseTitle: Agentic RL environments: sandboxes, masks and rewards
lessonTitle: Multi-turn rollouts: one sequence, two authors, one loss mask
md: A common bug: tokenizing the final transcript string again for training instead of keeping the exact token ids that were sampled. Re-tokenizing can merge tokens differently at the boundaries between model text and tool text, so the log-probabilities you train on no longer match the ones the policy produced, and the mask can land on the wrong positions.

courseTitle: AI and LLM security: prompt injection, agents and model risks
lessonTitle: Getting data out: images, links, tool calls
md: For every LLM feature, list the ways out: rendered images, links, tools that make network requests, and the user. Close the ones you do not need and allowlist the rest. Without a way out, stolen context stays put.

courseTitle: AI and LLM security: prompt injection, agents and model risks
lessonTitle: Data and model poisoning: backdoors you cannot see
md: Poisoning is a supply chain attack on data. Verify integrity with hashes, record provenance, and treat a model from an unknown trainer like a binary from an unknown publisher.

courseTitle: AI for materials discovery: stability, GNoME and MatterGen
lessonTitle: GNoME: active learning with DFT, and what counts as new
md: Active learning turns DFT from a verifier into a teacher: each round's results, including failures, retrain the filter, so the hit rate per DFT call keeps rising.

courseTitle: Watermarking AI outputs
lessonTitle: Distortion-free sampling: the Gumbel trick and SynthID tournaments
md: Distortion-free per token is not the same as diverse. Because r is a deterministic function of the key and the last few tokens, the same prompt and context always produce the same output, which a user who asks twice can notice. The next block shows Kuditipudi et al.'s fix.

courseTitle: Allocation tracing and replay
lessonTitle: Replaying workloads to compare allocators
md: Replay is open-loop: the program's computation between calls is gone, so cache contents and timing differ, and cycles per call in replay are not the application's allocator time. Use replay for memory comparisons and relative call costs, and confirm with a real run.

courseTitle: Anomaly and outlier detection
lessonTitle: Anomalies in time: seasonal baselines and robust residuals
md: Anomalies in the history contaminate the baseline. If last Tuesday's outage is in the training window, a mean-based baseline and standard deviation absorb it and become blind to the next one. That is why both the toy baseline here and S-H-ESD use medians and MAD: one bad day out of 27 does not move a same-hour median.

courseTitle: API security, OAuth and JWT
lessonTitle: Rate limits, quotas and resource exhaustion
md: Limits enforced only at one gateway disappear on any path that skips the gateway: a beta host, an internal route, an old API version. Apply the limit in the service, or make sure every route goes through the gateway.

courseTitle: API security, OAuth and JWT
lessonTitle: JWT anatomy: header, payload, signature and base64url
md: A JWT is readable by anyone and trustworthy only after the signature and claims are checked by the receiver, using keys and rules the receiver chose. Everything in it, including the header, is attacker-controlled until then.

courseTitle: Secure SDLC, code review and vulnerability management
lessonTitle: What an application security programme is, and who owns what
md: A programme is owners plus deadlines plus measurement. For every activity in this course, ask three questions: which named person or team does it, by when, and which number shows that it actually happens?

courseTitle: Secure SDLC, code review and vulnerability management
lessonTitle: SAST in CI: false positives, triage and developer trust
md: A suppression is a risk acceptance. If anyone can add `nosemgrep` without review, the cheapest way to pass CI is to silence the tool. Route suppressions in sensitive paths through CODEOWNERS (lesson 1) so AppSec sees them.

courseTitle: Secure SDLC, code review and vulnerability management
lessonTitle: Patch SLAs, exceptions and the race after disclosure
md: An exception without an expiry date is a permanent vulnerability with paperwork. Track exceptions as their own metric: how many, how old, and how many were renewed more than once.

courseTitle: Crash recovery (ARIES)
lessonTitle: Restart part 2: undo, CLRs, and crashing during recovery
md: Tuning tradeoffs follow directly from the passes. Rare checkpoints and slow background page writes make the smallest recLSN old, so redo scans more log. Long-running transactions make undo long and keep old log needed. Frequent checkpoints shorten redo but cost extra log and page writes at runtime.

courseTitle: Calling LLM APIs at scale: concurrency, rate limits, retries, caching
lessonTitle: Why a plain loop is too slow and a plain gather is too fast
md: A semaphore limits **how many** requests are in flight, not **how fast** they start. Concurrency times the inverse of latency gives your request rate, so when latency drops (short prompts, cache hits) the same semaphore sends requests faster. Pair it with a rate limiter, covered next.

courseTitle: Async runtimes (Tokio) and coroutines
lessonTitle: Cooperative scheduling: blocking, budgets and cancellation
md: Async Rust in one breath: `async fn` compiles to a lazy state machine; `poll` advances it until an await is Pending; the waker plus the epoll-based driver decide when to poll again; Tokio's workers spread tasks with local queues and stealing; and because nothing preempts a task, every task must reach a Pending await often, or move blocking work to `spawn_blocking`.

courseTitle: Audio embeddings and classification
lessonTitle: Embeddings as features: VGGish, YAMNet and PANNs
md: Split by clip (or by source recording), never by patch. Patches of one clip overlap by 50% and share the same label, so a random patch-level split puts near-copies in train and test and inflates accuracy. ESC-50 ships 5 folds for this reason, and the TensorFlow tutorial carries each clip's fold number along with every patch embedding and splits by fold.

courseTitle: Authentication and identity attacks
lessonTitle: Precomputed tables, rainbow tables, and why salts defeat them
md: A salt does nothing against an attacker focused on *one* account. With a single salted SHA-256 hash, the attacker simply runs their guess list with that salt at full GPU speed. Salting is necessary but not sufficient: the hash must also be slow, which is lesson 5.

courseTitle: Authentication and identity attacks
lessonTitle: Real-time phishing proxies and help-desk social engineering
md: Training people to spot fake pages helps, but NIST defines phishing resistance as working *without relying on the user's vigilance*. The Twitter employees were busy, remote, and called by someone who knew personal details about them.

courseTitle: Automotive and vehicle security
lessonTitle: Case: the 2015 Jeep, from head unit to CAN bus
md: A separate "safety" microcontroller adds no security if the internet-facing processor can rewrite its firmware. Count the trust boundary where verification happens, not where the chips are.

courseTitle: Autonomous research agents: plan, search, verify, evaluate
lessonTitle: Tokens, budgets and when to stop
md: Tokens buy research quality (80% of BrowseComp variance in Anthropic's analysis), so the budget is the main dial. Enforce budgets in the harness, reserve a share for synthesis and verification, and scale effort to the question.

courseTitle: Amazon Bedrock and the AWS generative AI stack
lessonTitle: Customizing models: fine-tuning, distillation, pretraining and import
md: Serving rules for custom models have changed over time. A 2023 AWS launch post said custom models needed Provisioned Throughput; current docs also offer on-demand custom model deployments, but only for listed base models and Regions. Check the current page before you promise a serving cost.

courseTitle: Binary reverse engineering: ARM64, compiled languages and firmware
lessonTitle: Putting it together: a workflow, language fingerprints and practice
md: Reverse engineering is compiler knowledge applied backwards. Each fingerprint, idiom and convention you learn from compiling your own code is one less guess when the source is gone.

courseTitle: 1.58-bit LLMs: ternary weights, BitLinear and bitnet.cpp
lessonTitle: Running ternary models fast: I2_S, lookup tables, real numbers
md: bitnet.cpp's kernels are **lossless**: they reproduce the training-time quantization exactly. On 1,000 prompts with a 700M BitNet b1.58 model, I2_S, TL1 and TL2 produced exactly the same output tokens (up to 100 per prompt) as an FP32 kernel 100% of the time, versus 1.4% for llama.cpp's own ternary formats TQ1_0 and TQ2_0, which quantize activations in 256-element blocks unlike training.

courseTitle: Branch prediction and branchless code
lessonTitle: Branchless code: cmov, masks and lookup tables
md: Branchless code trades a *possible* misprediction for *always* doing the work of both sides plus the select. Always check the compiler output (Compiler Explorer, the godbolt.org website that shows the assembly a compiler produces, or the `-S` flag, which makes the compiler write assembly instead of an object file) before hand-rewriting: the optimizer may already have done it, or may have a good reason not to.

courseTitle: Browser security internals: architecture, sandboxes and patch gaps
lessonTitle: JavaScript engines: tiers, shapes and stale assumptions
md: Misconception: "rewrite the engine in a memory-safe language and this goes away." The V8 sandbox post points out that when a compiler is part of the attack surface, a memory-safe implementation language cannot guarantee the code it *generates* is safe. That is why V8 adds containment (lesson 9) instead of relying on the language alone.

courseTitle: B-trees vs LSM-trees and compaction
lessonTitle: The LSM write path: memtable, flush and immutable SSTables
md: LSM reads search from newest to oldest and stop at the first entry for the key, whether that is a value or a tombstone. Correctness depends only on this ordering, never on old versions being gone.

courseTitle: Buffer pools and page eviction: CLOCK, LRU-K and 2Q
lessonTitle: LRU, CLOCK and PostgreSQL clock-sweep on a 4-frame pool
md: CLOCK is not "LRU but cheaper" in every case. It only approximates recency, and when all bits are set it evicts in plain circular order. Its win is that a hit costs one bit or counter update with no shared list to reorder.

courseTitle: Resilience, business continuity and disaster recovery
lessonTitle: MTD, RTO and RPO: the arithmetic and the dependency trap
md: RTO plus reprocessing time must fit inside the MTD. A service's achievable RTO is the longest path through its dependencies, so shared components inherit the shortest targets. State RPO per failure type: replication protects against losing a site, not against bad writes.

courseTitle: Resilience, business continuity and disaster recovery
lessonTitle: Designing the backup set: 3-2-1-1-0, schedules and retention
md: Choose the backup type by restore chain, the frequency by RPO, the retention by how late you will notice damage (by time, never by count), and the locations by failure domain, including the provider's own control plane. 3-2-1-1-0 adds an immutable copy and zero errors on verified restores.

courseTitle: Resilience, business continuity and disaster recovery
lessonTitle: Exercising the plan: tabletops, functional tests, failovers and chaos
md: Exercises fail when they are rigged to pass: announced weeks ahead, run by the people who wrote the plan, on a quiet Sunday, with the expert in the room. Inject realistic constraints (a key person unavailable, the wiki down, a backup from yesterday rather than an hour ago) and record measured times, not opinions.

courseTitle: Tokenizer-free and byte-level models
lessonTitle: Inside BLT: local encoder, latent Transformer, local decoder
md: Encoder: bytes plus hashed n-grams, pooled into patch vectors by masked cross-attention. Latent Transformer: the expensive part, once per patch. Decoder: bytes query the output of the patch before theirs to predict the next byte.

courseTitle: C and Rust: from malloc and free to ownership and unsafe
lessonTitle: The same bugs in Rust: compile errors, panics, and what slips through
md: Misconception: "Rust has no runtime checks, everything is proven at compile time." Lifetimes and aliasing are checked at compile time; indexing, `RefCell` borrows and debug-mode overflow are checked at run time. The design goal is that every remaining failure is defined, not that there are none.

courseTitle: C and Rust: from malloc and free to ownership and unsafe
lessonTitle: FFI: calling C from Rust without losing track of ownership
md: Undefined behavior does not stay on its side of the boundary. The Rust Reference notes that UB in a called C function makes the whole program undefined, including the Rust parts, and vice versa. FFI bindings are one of the most common reasons real code needs unsafe, so keep them thin and wrap them in a safe API.

courseTitle: Cache hierarchy (L1/L2/L3) and cache lines
lessonTitle: Writes, sharing between cores, and measuring your machine
md: Do not hard-code 64 just because it is common. Query the line size: Drepper suggests asking getconf for it at build time and handing it to the compiler as a macro definition (`-DCLS=$(getconf LEVEL1_DCACHE_LINESIZE)`), and if a binary must run everywhere, use the largest line size it may meet.

courseTitle: Circuit tracing and attribution graphs
lessonTitle: What attribution graphs found: arithmetic, languages, refusals, CoT
md: Confirmed by intervention: the addition lookup swap (1995 to 1998), the three multilingual edits, known-answer features gating hallucination, ablations that change refusals, and the hint-driven backward reasoning. Graph readings only: no carrying in the model's arithmetic, English as default, and anything involving attention, such as why the model attends to the hint or why "However" needs a new sentence.

courseTitle: Click models and unbiased learning to rank
lessonTitle: Small propensities, high variance, and clipping
md: Clipping changes what the estimator measures. A clipped rank is systematically undervalued, which pushes documents shown low back down, the same direction as the original position bias. Tune $\tau$ on held-out data and report it.

courseTitle: XSS, CSRF and client-side attacks
lessonTitle: Second lines of defence: strict CSP and Trusted Types
md: Trusted Types changes the review question from "is any of our thousands of DOM writes unsafe?" to "are our two or three policies correct?". The browser enforces that nothing else reaches a sink.

courseTitle: CLIP and image embeddings: learning vision from captions
lessonTitle: Image search with CLIP, the modality gap, and where it fails
md: Do not compare scores across modalities with one threshold. Image-image cosines and text-image cosines come from different regions of the space, so a cutoff tuned for text queries will not transfer to image queries, and a mixed index of image and text vectors will tend to rank same-modality items together.

courseTitle: Cloud detection and incident response
lessonTitle: Compromised instance forensics: protect, snapshot, memory, isolate
md: Misconception: "applying the quarantine security group cuts the attacker off". It stops new connections. Existing tracked connections continue until they time out, so verify with flow logs or host telemetry that the session actually ended, and use a network ACL or a stop when it has not.

courseTitle: Cloud security architecture: guardrails, serverless, attack paths
lessonTitle: Service control policies in depth: inheritance and exemptions
md: SCPs combine by intersection down the tree: an Allow is needed at every level, and a Deny at any level wins. Prefer deny-list SCPs on top of FullAWSAccess, exempt only named platform or break-glass roles through `aws:PrincipalArn`, and test every change in a staging OU first.

courseTitle: Cloud security architecture: guardrails, serverless, attack paths
lessonTitle: CSPM, CIEM and CNAPP, and a full architecture review
md: A good cloud architecture assumes one credential, one function or one account will fail, and makes sure that failure stays small: walls between accounts, guardrails nobody can lift, no hidden paths to admin, no standing human keys, logs and backups out of reach. Posture tools help you keep it that way; they do not design it for you.

courseTitle: Cloud security and IAM
lessonTitle: Storage exposure: public buckets, Block Public Access and SAS tokens
md: Turn on the provider's public-access guardrail at the highest level you can (organization or account), and treat any exception as a reviewed, documented decision. Then scan for anything public anyway: IAM Access Analyzer in AWS reports buckets shared publicly or with other accounts.

courseTitle: Clustering: k-means, DBSCAN and finding failure patterns
lessonTitle: Gaussian mixtures and EM: soft k-means with a shape per cluster
md: k-means is EM for a Gaussian mixture with one shared, fixed, vanishing round covariance. Free the covariances and you gain soft memberships and per-cluster shapes; you also gain more parameters to estimate, and a new way to fail.

courseTitle: Columnar storage and vectorized execution
lessonTitle: Why analytic scans want columns, not rows
md: Columns win when queries read few columns of many rows; rows win for point reads and frequent updates of whole records. The layout decides how many bytes a scan must move.

courseTitle: Compilers and optimization levels (-O2, LTO, inlining)
lessonTitle: Inside the optimizer: IR, SSA and the classic scalar passes
md: Misconception: "the optimizer understands what my code is for." It does not. Each pass applies one local rewrite it can prove safe, and the big wins come from chains: inlining exposes a constant, propagation folds it, DCE deletes the leftovers. When a chain breaks (a call it cannot see into, a pointer that might alias), every later step is lost.

courseTitle: Compilers and optimization levels (-O2, LTO, inlining)
lessonTitle: LTO and ThinLTO: optimizing across source files
md: Without LTO, a .c file is the optimizer's horizon. LTO stores the compiler's IR in the object files and optimizes the whole program at link time. ThinLTO does the global analysis on small summaries and the heavy work in parallel, so it scales and supports incremental builds.

courseTitle: Computer-use agents: seeing screens and driving mouse and keyboard
lessonTitle: Grounding: Set-of-Mark labels, DOM and accessibility trees
md: Misconception: Set-of-Mark always improves GUI grounding. Both SeeAct and OSWorld saw marks underperform richer text grounding on dense screens. Marks help most when there are few, well-separated elements.

courseTitle: Concurrency testing with loom and ThreadSanitizer
lessonTitle: ThreadSanitizer: catching races with vector clocks at runtime
md: TSan reports races that **did not cause a failure** in this run. It needs only that both conflicting accesses execute and that nothing orders them by happens-before. That is its big advantage over stress testing.

courseTitle: Consistency models: from linearizable to eventual
lessonTitle: Linearizability: one copy, respecting real time
md: A read that overlaps a write may return either the old or the new value. Once any read has returned the new value and completed, every later-starting read must return it too. Linearizability forbids the value from flickering back.

courseTitle: Consistent hashing and hot-key mitigation
lessonTitle: Consistent hashing with bounded loads: a hard cap per server
md: Bounded loads caps *load per server*, not *load per key*. If one key alone exceeds a server's capacity, forwarding spreads its requests across servers only when any server can answer for it, as with a cache that can fetch from the origin. A database shard that alone holds the data still needs the replication or splitting tools from the previous lesson.

courseTitle: Constraint satisfaction solvers: backtracking, AC-3, CDCL and CP-SAT
lessonTitle: Arc consistency: AC-3 prunes domains before guessing
md: Arc consistency is not the same as a solution. Three variables with domain $\{1,2\}$ and pairwise $\neq$ constraints are fully arc-consistent (every value has a support on every arc), yet no assignment satisfies all three. Propagation shrinks the search; it does not replace it.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: What ships in an image: base images, distroless and scanning
md: Ship the least software that runs your app: multi-stage builds into a minimal or distroless base, scanned in CI and rescanned while running.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: RBAC: roles, bindings and the permissions that escalate
md: RBAC only adds. Grant namespaced Roles with explicit resources, names and verbs. Treat Secrets list, pod creation, nodes/proxy, escalate, bind and impersonate as administrator-level rights.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: Secrets: base64 is not encryption
md: base64 hides nothing. Lock down who can get, list or watch Secrets and who can create pods, encrypt etcd data with a KMS provider, rewrite existing Secrets after enabling it, and keep high-value credentials in an external store.

courseTitle: Conversational query refinement: tracking search state across turns
lessonTitle: Why a multi-turn search needs explicit state
md: The state object, not the transcript, is the source of truth for what the user wants right now. The LLM proposes changes to it; code applies them; the query is a pure function of it.

courseTitle: Conversational query refinement: tracking search state across turns
lessonTitle: When to ask a clarifying question instead of guessing
md: Do not ask about what the state already answers, or about slots marked dontcare. Repeated or redundant questions are the fastest way to make mixed-initiative feel worse than a plain search box.

courseTitle: Chain-of-thought faithfulness and monitorability
lessonTitle: Do reasoning models admit the hints they use?
md: When the model can act on information without reasoning about it, its CoT usually stays silent about it, even with no pressure to hide. CoT monitoring then helps you notice frequent behaviors, but it cannot certify that a behavior is absent.

courseTitle: Chain-of-thought faithfulness and monitorability
lessonTitle: Why CoT is monitorable at all, and how to keep it so
md: A clean CoT is not evidence of safety for tasks that do not need a CoT. Chen et al. and Korbak et al. both warn that malign reasoning can happen in activations, so a monitoring-only safety case (an argument that a model is safe to deploy) fails there.

courseTitle: Cross-encoder rerankers: scoring query and document together
lessonTitle: Why a reranker reads the query and the document together
md: A cross-encoder is not a better embedding model. It has no vector output you could store in a vector database. If someone asks you to index a corpus with a reranker, the answer is that you cannot: the score exists only for a specific query.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: What cryptography promises, and to whom
md: Ask of every design: which of confidentiality, integrity and authenticity do I need, against whom, and where does the key live? A primitive that gives one goal never silently gives the others.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: Randomness: where keys come from, and the Debian disaster
md: A random-looking output says nothing about its entropy. Debian's weak keys passed every visual check; their weakness was only visible by counting how many could exist.

courseTitle: Using cryptography safely: how real systems got it wrong
lessonTitle: Fixed IVs in homemade protocols: Zerologon
md: An IV or nonce is an input with a contract (unique, sometimes unpredictable), not a constant. When a design fixes it, ask what the mode's security proof assumes, who controls the plaintext, and how many attempts an attacker gets. Better: use a standard authenticated protocol instead of designing one.

courseTitle: CUTLASS and CuTe: tiling GEMMs across the GPU memory hierarchy
lessonTitle: Why a fast GEMM is a hierarchy of tiles
md: Every level of the hierarchy does the same thing: stage a tile in a faster, smaller memory and reuse it across as many math operations as the capacity of that memory allows. Tile shapes are the main tuning knobs of a CUTLASS GEMM.

courseTitle: CUTLASS and CuTe: tiling GEMMs across the GPU memory hierarchy
lessonTitle: The CUTLASS 3.x API, epilogues and tuning tradeoffs
md: Fast CUTLASS kernels come from a few choices: tile shape (reuse versus occupancy and wave fit), stage count (latency hiding versus shared memory), kernel schedule (cooperative or ping-pong) and the epilogue fusion. CuTe layouts make each choice a type parameter instead of a rewrite.

courseTitle: CXL and memory disaggregation: far memory you can load and store
lessonTitle: Placing pages: tiering in Linux, pooling in Pond
md: CXL makes memory placement a policy problem again. The hardware gives you a slower, bigger NUMA tier; the operating system (tiering) or the cluster manager (pooling) must keep hot data local and push only cold or untouched data to it.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: The UK Computer Misuse Act, section by section
md: Under section 1 a failed attempt can be enough: the offence is about intent and knowledge, not success. 'I didn't get in' is not a defence to trying.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Export controls: Wassenaar and 'intrusion software'
md: "It's only code" is not an export defence. Sending exploit technology abroad can need a licence, and US rules also cover releasing controlled technology to foreign persons at home (a "deemed export", which the 2021 rule names). Disclosure to the people who will fix the bug is the carved-out case; selling capability is not.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Cover-ups and whistleblowing: Uber's CSO and Twitter's security lead
md: "Nobody asked me directly" is weak protection. Misprision is about *active concealment* of a known felony, and obstruction can be committed by causing others not to disclose. Changing records, drafting the NDA and signing statements you know mislead are acts, not silence.

courseTitle: Data mixing and curation: how DoReMi learns the pretraining mixture
lessonTitle: Upweighting means repeating: epochs, data limits and domain weights
md: Epochs = weight x budget / unique tokens. Up to about 4 epochs repetition costs almost nothing; beyond that each pass is worth less, and by about 40 it is worthless. Cap epochs per domain and give the surplus to domains that still have unique data.

courseTitle: Data-oriented design: struct-of-arrays vs array-of-structs
lessonTitle: Why a loop over objects wastes most of each cache line
md: Memory moves in cache lines. Lay out data so that the bytes a hot loop needs are packed together, and the bytes it skips live somewhere else.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: Classification: levels, impact and the high-water mark
md: Classify by the damage of disclosure (and of tampering or loss), not by how the data looks. Rate each information type, take the high-water mark for systems, and attach the result as a label that tools can read.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: How DLP recognises sensitive content
md: DLP is only as good as its detector's precision. Prefer labels and exact data match over generic patterns where you can; require context for high confidence; and measure precision on real traffic before turning on blocking. Hashed SSNs are not anonymous: with about a billion possible values, anyone holding the salt can hash them all, so guard the EDM hash file and salt as Restricted data.

courseTitle: Deception: honeypots, honeytokens and canaries
lessonTitle: Honeypots by interaction: low, medium and high
md: "High interaction" is not "better". It is more informative and more dangerous. Choose the lowest level that answers your question: for internal detection, a decoy that only needs to notice a login attempt does not need a real shell.

courseTitle: Deception: honeypots, honeytokens and canaries
lessonTitle: Legal, ethical and safety limits of deception
md: Before deploying a decoy, write down: who approved it, what it records, who can see that data and for how long, how it is contained, and the conditions under which it is switched off. Engage calls the last part gating criteria.

courseTitle: Deterministic simulation testing: replayable chaos in distributed code
lessonTitle: Why distributed bugs refuse to reproduce
md: DST makes a run a pure function of (code, seed). Faults can then be as aggressive and random as you like, because any failure they provoke can be replayed exactly by re-running one seed.

courseTitle: DevSecOps: CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure as code and policy as code
lessonTitle: CircleCI 2023: when the platform holding your secrets is breached
md: Encryption at rest did not save the secrets, because a running service must decrypt them to use them, and the attacker read the keys from a running process. The only secret a breached CI vendor cannot leak is one it never stored.

courseTitle: Diffusion language models: generating text by unmasking
lessonTitle: Sampling: predict every mask, keep the confident, remask the rest
md: A sampling step is: one forward pass over the whole sequence, a guess at every masked slot, then keep the k most confident guesses and remask the rest. The schedule fixes k per step; the confidence ranking decides the order.

courseTitle: Disaggregated prefill and decode
lessonTitle: Why prefill stalls decode on a shared GPU
md: Prefill is compute-bound and sets TTFT; decode is memory-bound and sets TPOT. Putting both in one batch makes each phase pay for the other.

courseTitle: Disaggregated prefill and decode
lessonTitle: Chunked prefill or disaggregation: when each one wins
md: Disaggregation adds failure modes. DistServe notes a fault in one decode instance that serves several prefill instances can spread, and FCFS prefill can create a convoy effect where long prompts block short ones. Mooncake must sometimes reject a request after its prefill if no decode slot is left, wasting that prefill. Lesson 5 covers leases, lost transfers and failure policies.

courseTitle: Disk, file system and mobile forensics
lessonTitle: Carving: recovering files with no metadata at all
md: A carved file has no name, no path, no timestamps and no owner. You can testify that these bytes were on the disk at this offset. Who created them, and when, needs other evidence.

courseTitle: DiskANN and CAGRA: billion-scale ANN on SSDs and GPUs
lessonTitle: Why a billion vectors break in-memory graph indexes
md: Two numbers drive an SSD-resident index: **total reads per query** (limits throughput, since the SSD has a fixed IOPS budget) and **round trips per query** (limits latency, since each trip costs a few hundred microseconds). DiskANN attacks both: a graph with short search paths, and a search that issues several reads per round trip.

courseTitle: DPO and its variants: preference tuning without RL
lessonTitle: When preferences look certain: DPO overfits, IPO holds
md: Do not read DPO's $\beta$ as a guarantee of staying close to the reference. On pairs the model already separates, DPO's gradient shrinks but never pushes back, so drift continues as long as you keep training. The IPO paper notes that early stopping is the usual extra guard.

courseTitle: Online data migration (dual-write and backfill)
lessonTitle: Backfilling history without overwriting newer writes
md: A backfill copy is always an *old* view of a row. Whatever mechanism you use (insert-if-absent, versions, or watermarks), it must guarantee that a backfilled row can never land after a newer write for the same key, and that deletes are remembered.

courseTitle: End-to-end encrypted messaging: Signal protocol and MLS
lessonTitle: Why one long-term key is not enough: forward secrecy and prekeys
md: Forward secrecy needs keys that are deleted. Prekeys let the offline party contribute a fresh, later-deleted key to the first message, which is what makes asynchronous forward secrecy possible.

courseTitle: End-to-end encrypted messaging: Signal protocol and MLS
lessonTitle: Safety numbers: checking that the server gave you the right key
md: A safety number is a hash of both identity keys. Matching numbers prove both apps hold the same two keys; a server that substituted keys cannot make them match without breaking SHA-512 or the curve.

courseTitle: End-to-end encrypted messaging: Signal protocol and MLS
lessonTitle: When protocols broke: Matrix (2022) and Threema (2023)
md: The Threema authors' lessons apply to every messenger: good libraries do not make a good protocol ("don't roll your own cryptographic protocol"), beware cross-protocol interactions and use separate keys for separate purposes, and analyse a design formally before release rather than patching after breaks.

courseTitle: eBPF tracing with bpftrace: probes, verifier, maps
lessonTitle: The verifier: proving every path safe before it runs
md: The verifier runs once, at load time, and proves properties of **all** paths: bounded execution, typed pointers, null checks before dereference, initialized registers, in-bounds stack and map access. Because the proof is done up front, the JIT-compiled code needs no runtime checks and runs at native speed.

courseTitle: Edge devices and exposure management: VPNs, firewalls and appliances
lessonTitle: Edge devices: the doors attackers now try first
md: An edge appliance combines the three things attackers want most: anyone can talk to it before logging in, it holds credentials with reach inside, and it is usually the least observed computer you own.

courseTitle: Edge devices and exposure management: VPNs, firewalls and appliances
lessonTitle: Management interfaces: keep the admin door off the internet
md: The service may need the internet; the admin interface does not. Put management on its own network or behind a separate enforcement point, and prove it with an outside scan.

courseTitle: Efficient reasoning: overthinking and length control
lessonTitle: Why RL makes reasoning long: the length bias in the policy loss
md: Response length growth during RL is partly an optimizer artifact. Check the loss normalization (a constant normalizer as in Dr. GRPO, $\lambda < 1$ for PPO) and the mix of solvable problems before adding a length penalty, and log length separately for correct and incorrect rollouts.

courseTitle: Efficient reasoning: overthinking and length control
lessonTitle: Whether to think at all: NoThinking, hybrid modes and routing
md: The modes are far apart on hard problems. Qwen3-235B-A22B scored 85.7 on AIME 2024 thinking and 40.1 without. Fusion also had a price: for Qwen3-32B, thinking-mode AIME 2024 fell from 83.8 to 81.4 after the fusion and general-RL stages. A user-chosen switch is only as good as the user's guess about difficulty.

courseTitle: Encodings, parsers and Unicode attacks
lessonTitle: Unicode normalisation: NFC, NFD, NFKC and NFKD
md: UAX #15: "Normalization Forms KC and KD must not be blindly applied to arbitrary text", because they erase distinctions that can matter. Use NFKC (usually with case folding, next lesson) for identifiers such as usernames, and NFC for stored text you will show back to people.

courseTitle: Encodings, parsers and Unicode attacks
lessonTitle: XML, multipart forms and email addresses: same bytes, different trees
md: For every structured format: one strict parser at the boundary, reject anything ambiguous (duplicate fields, malformed headers, unknown XML structure), and pass the parsed result, not the original bytes, to the rest of the system.

courseTitle: How EDR works: telemetry, ETW, Sysmon and endpoint hardening
lessonTitle: Process injection as telemetry: Sysmon events 8, 10 and 25
md: Misconception: "a GrantedAccess of 0x1FFFFF on LSASS is always an attack." Security products, backup agents and admin tools often request all access. Context decides: which signed program, how often, from which path, and with which call trace. Baseline the normal requesters on your hosts, then alert on the rest.

courseTitle: Energy disaggregation (NILM): from Hart's edges to seq2point
lessonTitle: One meter, many appliances: the disaggregation problem
md: NILM is an inverse problem: one observed sum, many hidden parts. Every algorithm you will meet differs only in what extra knowledge it uses to choose among the many decompositions that add up to the same total.

courseTitle: Entity normalization: job titles, schools and companies
lessonTitle: Blocking: compare only pairs that could match
md: A pair that blocking drops is classified as a non-match without ever being looked at. No scoring model can recover it. Use several strict rules joined by OR (Splink's advice: a longer list of strict rules beats a short list of loose ones), so a typo in one field is caught by a rule on another.

courseTitle: Entity normalization: job titles, schools and companies
lessonTitle: Evaluating entity resolution: labels, pairwise and cluster metrics
md: Pairwise metrics are dominated by large clusters: a 100-record entity implies 4,950 pairs, a 2-record entity one pair. On skewed data, a model can improve pairwise F1 while breaking many small entities. Always pair it with a per-record or per-cluster metric.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Who runs the tenant: Entra roles, Global Administrator and PIM
md: Count who can become Global Administrator, not only who is one: role assigners, admin credential resetters, app credential managers and hybrid identity admins. Keep the count small, make it eligible rather than active, and keep two tested emergency accounts outside it.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Entra tokens: lifetimes, refresh tokens and revocation
md: Entra access is a chain: a 60 to 90 minute access token renewed by a 90-day refresh token that is bound to user and client, not to a resource. Revocation cuts the chain; CAE cuts the current link at Exchange, SharePoint, Teams and Graph.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Conditional Access in Entra: baselines and the gaps attackers use
md: A Conditional Access policy set is only as strong as what it does not cover. Inventory the exclusions, the service principals and the allowed flows, block legacy authentication and device code, and test every change in report-only mode first.

courseTitle: epoll and event loops: serving many sockets from one thread
lessonTitle: Why one thread per connection stops scaling
md: **Readiness notification**: you give the kernel a set of file descriptors and it tells you which ones can do I/O right now without blocking. You still perform the `read` or `write` yourself. An **event loop** is a thread that repeatedly waits for readiness, then runs a short handler (a *callback*) for each ready descriptor.

courseTitle: Avoiding overfitting to a public query set
lessonTitle: Adaptive overfitting: how score feedback leaks the test set
md: Do not read those results as "test reuse is safe." ImageNet's test set has tens of thousands of images and Kaggle private splits often thousands of rows. Search teams often tune against 50 to 200 queries with free-form changes (prompts, thresholds, filters). That is exactly the small-n, many-k regime where the toy overfits.

courseTitle: Exploit mitigations: ASLR, DEP, canaries and CFI
lessonTitle: From bug to control: why exploit mitigations exist
md: Common misconception: "the binary has every mitigation enabled, so this overflow is not a security issue." Every mitigation in this course has a known bypass class (lesson 14), and real exploits combine several bugs to get past them. An overflow is a security bug whether or not today's exploit techniques reach it.

courseTitle: False sharing and cache-line padding
lessonTitle: Four independent counters that refuse to scale
md: Correct code can still have false sharing. Tests pass, there is no race for a sanitizer (a race detector such as ThreadSanitizer, which flags conflicting unsynchronized accesses to the same memory) to report, and the profile only shows a slow, innocent-looking loop. It is found by measuring, not by reading for bugs.

courseTitle: Federated learning: training without moving the data
lessonTitle: Cheaper rounds and smarter servers: compression and FedOpt
md: Compression is lossy, and lossy is only safe when it is **unbiased**. Probabilistic quantization and scaled subsampling are unbiased per client, so their errors average out across a round. A biased compressor (rounding to nearest, keeping only the largest entries) pushes every client the same way, which looks like drift in disguise.

courseTitle: Filtered ANN with ACORN: predicate subgraph traversal
lessonTitle: Why a filter breaks greedy search on an HNSW graph
md: Predicate subgraph traversal is the right search strategy (no distance computations wasted on failing nodes), but on a normal HNSW graph the predicate subgraph is sparse and disconnected. ACORN changes how the graph is built, or how neighbors are looked up, so that the predicate subgraph stays connected for any predicate.

courseTitle: Fine-grained MoE, shared experts, aux-loss-free load balancing
lessonTitle: Build it: a DeepSeekMoE layer with bias balancing in your GPT
md: Do not read quality conclusions off a run this small. Character-level Shakespeare with a 3.65M-parameter MoE (0.9M active) trains in under an hour per run on a CPU; differences of a few thousandths in validation loss between configurations are within seed noise. What this lab shows reliably is the mechanism: what the router does without balancing, and how each method changes the expert loads.

courseTitle: Firmware and boot security: UEFI, Secure Boot and bootkits
lessonTitle: Case: Baton Drop and BlackLotus, a signed door left open
md: "Fixed" and "no longer trusted" are different states. Until the vulnerable signed binary is revoked or rolled past, the fix protects only machines whose attacker politely uses the new file.

courseTitle: FlashAttention-3 and FlashAttention-4
lessonTitle: FlashAttention-2 kernel tile by tile: forward, backward, parallelism
md: Every later kernel is this loop. FlashAttention-3's producer warps load $K_j, V_j$ and its pipeline overlaps the next $S_{ij}$ with the current $PV$; FlashAttention-4 moves $S$ and $P$ out of registers into a new on-chip memory, pairs thread blocks for the five backward matmuls, and orders causal tiles longest first (lessons 6 to 8). Only the mapping onto hardware changes.

courseTitle: FlashInfer: an attention engine for LLM serving
lessonTitle: Tile sizes, GQA head fusion and JIT attention variants
md: The paper's design in one line: one block-sparse view of every KV layout, attention states merged exactly so work can be split and composed freely, a per-step plan that balances skewed lengths while staying CUDA-graph friendly, and a JIT template so new variants get fused kernels instead of new libraries.

courseTitle: Formal methods for security: protocol proofs and verified systems
lessonTitle: Three messages, seventeen years: Lowe's attack on Needham-Schroeder
md: Protocol attacks rarely break cryptography. They abuse the logic: a message that can be replayed, forwarded or reinterpreted in another run. The defence is to bind every message to its context (who sent it, to whom, in which run) and to check that binding by machine, not by eye.

courseTitle: Formal methods for security: protocol proofs and verified systems
lessonTitle: Verified kernels and compilers: seL4's security proofs and CompCert
md: A verified system is a chain: properties, specification, code, compiler, hardware. Every link that is proved is strong; every link that is assumed or unverified (front-end, assembly, hardware model, timing) is where the remaining bugs live. When you read "formally verified", ask for the list of assumptions; good projects publish one.

courseTitle: Formal verification of systems code (TLA+, Verus)
lessonTitle: Refinement: proving a detailed design implements an abstract one
md: Implementation is implication: the detailed spec, seen through a refinement mapping, must allow only behaviors the abstract spec allows. Extra internal steps are fine because they map to stuttering steps.

courseTitle: FP8 and FP4 training: E4M3, scaling, MXFP4 and NVFP4
lessonTitle: What 8 and 4 bits can hold: E4M3, E5M2 and E2M1
md: Exponent bits buy **range**, mantissa bits buy **precision**. E4M3 rounds with at most 6.25% relative error but spans only about 18 binades; E5M2 spans about 32 binades at 12.5%; E2M1 (FP4) spans 3.58 binades at up to 25%.

courseTitle: FP8 and FP4 training: E4M3, scaling, MXFP4 and NVFP4
lessonTitle: NVFP4: 16-value blocks, E4M3 scales and a tensor scale
md: In NVFP4 the amax of every 16-value block is encoded at close to FP8 precision (the block scale is E4M3), which is at least 1/16 = 6.25% of all values. MXFP4 stores every value, the amax included, at FP4 precision behind a power-of-two scale.

courseTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust-and-safety engineering
lessonTitle: Network and device signals: IPs, proxies and fingerprints
md: Never trust a device signal you did not verify. A header or a JavaScript value is a claim made by the client. Use it to raise suspicion when claims disagree or repeat across many accounts, not to grant trust on its own.

courseTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust-and-safety engineering
lessonTitle: Promotion and referral abuse: multi-accounting and holds
md: Every promotion is a price per account. Tie it to a scarce identity, check the link between referrer and referee, and hold the payout until the qualifying payment can no longer be reversed.

courseTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust-and-safety engineering
lessonTitle: From risk score to decision: rules, models, step-up and review
md: Pick actions by expected cost: allow when $pL$ is small, block when $(1-p)G$ is small, and step up in between when the challenge catches more fraud than it costs in lost customers.

courseTitle: fsync, write-ahead logs and group commit
lessonTitle: Why write() returning does not mean your data is safe
md: Calling fsync on a file does not necessarily make the file's **directory entry** durable. A newly created or renamed file also needs an fsync on a file descriptor for the directory, or after a crash the name may be missing.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: A real hunt with libFuzzer: harness, run log and the crash
md: A harness plus a sanitizer turns 'run the parser on generated bytes' into an automatic bug finder: coverage guidance reaches deep code, comparison tracing gets past magic values, and ASan converts silent corruption into a report with a saved reproducer.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: Protocol and stateful fuzzing, and the Broadcom Wi-Fi case
md: Stateful targets need stateful fuzzing: keep a valid prefix, mutate later messages, use responses or coverage to recognise new states, and reset the target between sequences. Firmware that skips basic mitigations (no stack cookies) makes every such bug worse.

courseTitle: Fuzzy matching and string similarity
lessonTitle: Filling the Wagner-Fischer table cell by cell
md: The table gives one number, but several different edit sequences can tie for the minimum. The traceback picks one of them. Do not read a single alignment as *the* explanation of how two strings differ.

courseTitle: Fuzzy matching and string similarity
lessonTitle: Indexes that skip most strings: trigram filters and BK-trees
md: Both indexes trade exactness of the first step for speed: a trigram index proposes candidates by a cheap overlap count, a BK-tree rules out subtrees with the triangle inequality. Neither changes the final score; you still verify candidates with the metric you trust.

courseTitle: Geometric hashing and star-pattern plate solving
lessonTitle: The Astrometry.net quad code, computed step by step
md: Invariant does not mean mirror-proof. Some cameras and optical paths flip the image. Astrometry.net's code-flip helper swaps each (x, y) pair, and the solver defaults to trying both parities (parity here means whether the image is mirrored or not). Groth's triangle method instead records whether vertices run clockwise and accepts either sense.

courseTitle: Geospatial indexing and geo filters
lessonTitle: Radius search: cover with cells, then check exact distance
md: `WHERE ST_Distance(a, b) < 500` gives the right answer but cannot use the spatial index, so it scans every row. The PostGIS docs pair them deliberately: use `ST_DWithin` to limit the search with the index, then `ST_Distance` only for sorting the few survivors.

courseTitle: GPU memory allocators and suballocation
lessonTitle: Why frameworks do not call cudaMalloc for every tensor
md: Misconception: "nvidia-smi shows 20 GB used, so my tensors use 20 GB." It shows reserved memory plus the CUDA context: the driver's per-process state on the GPU, such as loaded kernel code and the driver's own buffers, which uses device memory that PyTorch's counters never include. Compare `memory_allocated()` with `memory_reserved()` before hunting for a leak.

courseTitle: GPU memory hierarchy and coalescing
lessonTitle: From registers to HBM: the GPU memory map
md: **Local memory is not local to the chip.** The word refers to scope (one thread), not location. Spilled registers, large per-thread arrays and arrays indexed with values the compiler cannot resolve at compile time all go to local memory, which has the latency and bandwidth of global memory.

courseTitle: GPU memory hierarchy and coalescing
lessonTitle: Case study: one matrix transpose, three kernels
md: The NVIDIA post's conclusion: coalescing global memory accesses is by far the most critical step. Use shared memory to turn strided global access into coalesced access, then check the shared access for bank conflicts.

courseTitle: GPU profiling and speed-of-light analysis with Nsight
lessonTitle: How profiling perturbs what it measures
md: Decide which question you are asking before you choose the flags. Isolated-kernel analysis wants the defaults: locked clocks, flushed caches, serialized launches. System-representative behavior wants `--replay-mode application --clock-control none --cache-control none`. Mixing the two across runs produces numbers that disagree for reasons that have nothing to do with your code.

courseTitle: GraphRAG: entity graphs, communities, and global search
lessonTitle: From chunks to an entity graph with LLM extraction
md: The graph is an LLM's *abstractive summary* of the corpus (written in the model's own words, not copied sentences), not a parse of it. Every node and edge carries an LLM-written description, and those descriptions, not the raw text, are what later stages summarize.

courseTitle: GRPO and RLVR: RL with verifiable rewards
lessonTitle: RLVR: replacing the reward model with a program
md: Verifiable does not mean perfect. A verifier can reject correct answers (12.0 versus 12) or accept wrong ones (a unit-test suite that misses edge cases). Real pipelines normalize answers; for example, Tulu 3's 'flex' MATH evaluation tries three different ways to extract the final answer, because models often ignore the requested format. The quality of the checker caps the quality of the signal.

courseTitle: Transit feeds: GTFS Schedule and GTFS Realtime
lessonTitle: What a GTFS Schedule zip contains and how its tables join
md: A stop can appear twice in one trip, for example on a loop route where the bus starts and ends at the same stop. That is why `stop_sequence`, not `stop_id`, identifies a row of a trip. Code that keys stop times by `stop_id` alone silently overwrites one visit with the other.

courseTitle: A history of hacking: landmark incidents and what they changed
lessonTitle: Phone phreaking: when the voice line was also the control line
md: Filtering out the 2600 Hz tone would have been a weak fix: phreaks used many other tones, and a filter on a shared channel is always a race. Removing the attacker's access to the control channel ended the whole class of trick.

courseTitle: A history of hacking: landmark incidents and what they changed
lessonTitle: Conficker: the botnet that made the industry organise
md: Conficker showed both sides of collective defence: an industry coalition could deny a botnet its control channel at internet scale, but cleaning millions of unmanaged PCs was beyond it. Patching (MS08-067 was a month old) and removing risky defaults (AutoRun) would have prevented most infections.

courseTitle: A history of hacking: landmark incidents and what they changed
lessonTitle: SolarWinds and Log4Shell: what you install and what you import
md: SolarWinds attacked what you install (a trusted vendor's build), Log4Shell lived in what you import (a free library inside other products). The responses were inventory (SBOMs), verifiable builds, least privilege for powerful tools like network monitors, and review boards that turn incidents into public lessons.

courseTitle: Side channels and hardware security
lessonTitle: What a side channel is: secrets leaking through how code runs
md: A side-channel attack does not break the mathematics. It breaks the assumption that an implementation reveals only its outputs. Every defence in this course makes some byproduct independent of the secret, hides the secret from the computation that leaks, or keeps the observer away.

courseTitle: HTTP request smuggling and web cache attacks
lessonTitle: One request, two readers: why proxies and caches disagree
md: Testing a site's proxies or cache for these bugs can harm *other* users, because the leftover bytes or poisoned entries land on real people. Test only systems you own or have written permission to test, and prefer your own lab: the toys in this course run entirely in one Python process.

courseTitle: HTTP request smuggling and web cache attacks
lessonTitle: How HTTP caches decide: keys, freshness and Vary
md: A cache key is a promise: "any two requests with this key deserve the same response". Every attack in the next lessons breaks that promise, either because the response depended on something outside the key, or because two different resources ended up under one key.

courseTitle: Huge pages: 2 MiB and 1 GiB mappings, hugetlbfs and THP
lessonTitle: hugetlbfs: a reserved pool you map on purpose
md: A pool is memory you have given away. Those 3170 pages hold 6.2 GiB out of the page cache (the kernel's in-memory cache of file data) and away from every other process whether or not PostgreSQL is running. Over-sizing `nr_hugepages` is a common way to cause out-of-memory kills on a box that looks half empty.

courseTitle: Hybrid attention and SSM models
lessonTitle: Counting cache bytes: growing KV cache plus a fixed state
md: Hybrids do not help much at short context. At 1,024 tokens the cache formula gives only about 1.9x less memory for Nemotron-H-8B, and both the Jamba and NVIDIA papers report similar speed to Transformers at small context lengths. The gains grow with context and batch size.

courseTitle: Hybrid search: fusing BM25 and dense retrieval
lessonTitle: Lab: build and measure a hybrid pipeline on SciFact
md: Measure complementarity before fusing: each retriever's recall@100, their overlap and the recall of the union, which caps fusion and reranking. Tune on one split, report on another, test per-query differences, and measure every stage: in our SciFact run a small MS MARCO cross-encoder undid the fusion gain.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: What OT and ICS are, and why they are not just IT
md: IT protects data; OT protects people, equipment and the process. The order of priorities is different (safety and availability first), and every defence in this course is shaped by that.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: Case: Stuxnet, the controller that lied
md: Stuxnet attacked at the two places defenders trusted most: the engineering software (so the program looked unchanged) and the operator's view (so the process looked normal). The defence is verification through a path the attacker does not control.

courseTitle: SSO and federation: SAML, OIDC, SCIM and Golden SAML
lessonTitle: One login, many apps: identity providers, service providers and trust
md: Federation replaces many passwords with one trust decision per app: accept whatever this IdP's key signs, after checking it was meant for me, now. Every attack in this course breaks one of those three parts: the key, the checks, or the moment.

courseTitle: SSO and federation: SAML, OIDC, SCIM and Golden SAML
lessonTitle: Setting up trust: metadata, signing certificates and key rollover
md: Treat the IdP's signing keys and the configuration that says which IdPs and keys are trusted as tier 0 (Microsoft's name for the assets that control every identity in an organisation): the same protection as domain controllers (the servers that hold Active Directory's accounts and keys). Anyone who can change either can become any user without touching a password.

courseTitle: Identity governance and privileged access management
lessonTitle: Who has access, why, and who said so: identity governance
md: Identity governance answers: should this access exist, who decided, and can we prove it? Every entitlement should trace to a rule or an approved request, and the authoritative record (usually HR) drives the rest.

courseTitle: Identity governance and privileged access management
lessonTitle: Privileged access workstations and the clean source rule
md: Session security cannot exceed device security. PAM, bastions and JIT protect the path; the PAW protects its start. Decide at a policy engine using identity, device and approval together, issue short-lived credentials, and enforce at one point.

courseTitle: Image alignment (homography) and change detection
lessonTitle: Differencing and picking a threshold with Otsu's method
md: Otsu turns threshold selection into a 1D search over the histogram: maximize $\omega_0\omega_1(\mu_0-\mu_1)^2$. It works well when changed and unchanged pixels form two separated groups, and only then.

courseTitle: Incident response and digital forensics
lessonTitle: Containment: isolate, watch, disable, block, and the trade-offs
md: Isolating a host is not the same as stopping damage on it. NIST's example: a process that pings a remote host and, when the ping fails after disconnection, encrypts the disk. Capture what you need first when you can.

courseTitle: Incident response and digital forensics
lessonTitle: Ransomware response: pay or not, law enforcement and sanctions
md: Do not read the casino pair as "paying works". As one threat analyst quoted by The Register put it, the incidents are not necessarily comparable: we do not know their scope or which systems and backups were hit. And paying did not stop Caesars' data theft or its notification duties.

courseTitle: Injection: when data becomes code
lessonTitle: Parameterised queries: code and data on separate channels
md: Parameterise every value. Map every identifier and keyword through a fixed allowlist. Never quote a placeholder: in SQLite, `'?'` inside quotes is just a one-character string, and the call fails with "Incorrect number of bindings supplied"; Django's documentation warns against the same mistake with `'%s'`.

courseTitle: io_uring: asynchronous I/O through shared rings
lessonTitle: Fixed resources, polling, multishot networking and tradeoffs
md: SQPOLL is not a free "go faster" switch. The poll thread consumes a CPU while it spins. io_uring_sqpoll(7) warns it can hurt low-IOPS (few I/O operations per second), bursty or CPU-bound workloads and that it only speeds up submission, not completion handling. Benchmark with and without it.

courseTitle: IoT and embedded device security
lessonTitle: Device secrets: per-device keys, secure elements and House of Keys
md: Design rule: the worst outcome of fully compromising one unit should be the loss of that unit. Achieve it with per-device keys generated on the device, public keys in the cloud, and no shared secrets in firmware.

courseTitle: JavaScript and Node.js security
lessonTitle: Prototype pollution: one request changes every object
md: `--disable-proto` is a useful second layer, not the fix: our test shows the `constructor.prototype` route still pollutes with it on. Fix the write (own keys, refused names, null-prototype objects); add the flag as defence in depth.

courseTitle: JavaScript and Node.js security
lessonTitle: The server-client boundary: Server Actions, secrets and bundles
md: Do not treat arguments of a Server Action as typed or trusted because TypeScript declared their types. TypeScript types disappear at run time; the POST body can contain anything. Validate arguments with a schema inside the action, exactly as you would for a REST endpoint.

courseTitle: Jepsen-style fault testing: nemeses, histories and checkers
lessonTitle: Why a healthy cluster hides consistency bugs
md: Jepsen judges a system only by its history: what clients asked for and what they were told. A violation is reported only when **no** legal execution of the claimed model could explain that history, so a failure is a real bug, not a guess.

courseTitle: Kernel autotuning and configuration search
lessonTitle: Search strategies and the trial budget
md: Match the strategy to the budget. Under about 20 trials, use a ranking (a heuristic, a cost model, or a curated list) and measure its top few. From tens to a few hundred, random sampling is a strong and honest baseline. Past a few hundred, evolutionary or local refinement pays off, and a learned model pays off at every budget.

courseTitle: Kernel bypass: driving NICs and NVMe from user space (DPDK, SPDK)
lessonTitle: The price of bypass, and when to choose something else
md: Two folk beliefs ixy tested and found weak: bigger rings do not add throughput (they add latency), and huge pages inside the driver itself changed throughput by only 1 to 3% at realistic ring sizes (5.5% at the largest). That test ran without the IOMMU. With the IOMMU on, ixy lost 62% of throughput on 4 KiB pages (the IOMMU's small TLB thrashes) and nothing on 2 MiB pages, so hugepages still matter a lot.

courseTitle: Windows kernel and driver security: BYOVD and kernel hardening
lessonTitle: When the signing pipeline is the target: ADV220005
md: Every signature-based trust decision has an upstream: the people and processes that issue signatures. When that upstream is abused (stolen keys, fraudulent developer accounts), revocation, deny lists and inventory-based allowlists are what still work.

courseTitle: Kernel fusion: moving fewer bytes through HBM
lessonTitle: Why chains of elementwise ops are memory bound
md: Misconception: "the GPU is slow at GELU because tanh is expensive". Profile first. A standalone GELU kernel on a large tensor is limited by the read and the write of the tensor, not by tanh.

courseTitle: Knowledge distillation: teaching a small model with a big one
lessonTitle: A patient and consistent teacher: the recipe that makes KD work
md: Caching teacher outputs is only safe when the student's input is exactly the cached input. With random crops, flips, noise or mixup on the student side, cache the augmentation too or run the teacher live on the same batch. For language models the input is the token sequence itself, so the same rule says: teacher and student must score the same tokens.

courseTitle: Knowledge distillation: teaching a small model with a big one
lessonTitle: When distillation works, when it fails, and what it costs
md: Distillation trades extra training compute (running a teacher) for a cheaper model to serve. It works best when the student can realistically imitate the teacher; when the gap is large, shrink it with an assistant or an easier teacher.

courseTitle: KV cache compression and quantization
lessonTitle: Beyond rounding: pre-RoPE keys, outliers, and FP8 in production
md: FP8 without calibration uses a scale of 1.0. That works when values fit FP8's range, but calibrated scales are what vLLM recommends for best accuracy, and some layers (such as sliding-window ones, which attend only to a fixed number of recent tokens) can be kept in the native dtype, the model's own number format.

courseTitle: KV cache compression and quantization
lessonTitle: Build and test it: quantize real keys, then evict on a needle test
md: These numbers are one run: one small model, one synthetic task, a 2K-token prompt and 50 trials per bar, so other keys or filler can move a bar by several points. They show failure modes, not rankings: repeated filler is unusually easy for StreamingLLM and unusually hard for windowed voting. Rerun the harness on your own prompts, lengths and model before choosing a method.

courseTitle: KV cache offloading: tiers, reload vs recompute, capacity and reuse
lessonTitle: Finding a prefix across tiers, requests and engines
md: A cached block after a gap is useless for this request. KV at position 7 depends on every earlier token through attention in every layer, so if block 6 must be recomputed, block 7 must be too, even if an identical hash for it were stored. Eviction that removes a middle block silently strands everything after it.

courseTitle: Clocks: Lamport, vector and hybrid logical clocks
lessonTitle: Lamport clocks: a counter that respects happened-before
md: Lamport clocks do not detect concurrency. From $L(a) < L(b)$ you may conclude only that b did not happen before a. Any code that treats a larger Lamport timestamp as "definitely caused by" is wrong.

courseTitle: Late interaction: ColBERT, PLAID and ColPali
lessonTitle: Searching millions of passages: candidates, centroids, PLAID
md: Cheap approximate scores filter, exact scores decide. PLAID is the same funnel as BM25 followed by a cross-encoder, built inside one model: centroid ids are the cheap representation and decompressed vectors are the precise one.

courseTitle: Latent reasoning: chain of continuous thought (Coconut)
lessonTitle: Build Coconut: stage data, loss mask and the multi-pass forward
md: A Coconut training step is n + 1 cached forward passes whose logits are joined into one loss. Gradients flow back through every pass, so time and stored activations both grow with the number of thoughts.

courseTitle: Learned indexes: replacing B-tree search with a fitted model
lessonTitle: An index is a model: predicting where a key sits
md: A learned range index is a model of the key CDF plus two stored numbers per model, min_err and max_err. The model makes a guess; the error bounds turn the guess into a guarantee for every stored key.

courseTitle: Learned sparse retrieval with SPLADE
lessonTitle: Why learn sparse vectors instead of dense ones
md: A learned sparse vector is still a bag of weighted terms, so it can live in a normal inverted index. The transformer only decides *which* terms get *how much* weight, including terms absent from the text.

courseTitle: Learning to rank: from RankNet to LambdaMART
lessonTitle: LambdaMART: boosted trees that fit the lambdas
md: LambdaMART = gradient boosted regression trees whose regression targets are the LambdaRank lambdas, recomputed after re-sorting at every round.

courseTitle: Linear attention and Gated DeltaNet
lessonTitle: Chunkwise DeltaNet derived: WY form and the UT transform by hand
md: The WY form and the UT transform turn C sequential rank-1 updates into one small C x C triangular solve plus matmuls ($KK^\top$, $TK$, $TV$, $WS^\top$, $QK^\top$, $D^\top K$). Only that solve and the hand-off of the state between chunks remain sequential.

courseTitle: Linux for security: users, permissions, processes and logs
lessonTitle: Setuid, setgid and sticky: borrowed privilege and its bugs
md: "It is only a local bug" is a dangerous phrase. Local privilege escalation means any foothold, such as a hijacked web application running as `www-data`, becomes root. PwnKit and Dirty COW both needed only an ordinary account.

courseTitle: Linux for security: users, permissions, processes and logs
lessonTitle: Reading Linux logs: journald, auth.log, failed logins and sudo
md: Learn the shape of four lines: Failed password, Accepted (password or publickey), sudo COMMAND, and sudo denials. Then look for sequences, not single lines: failures then success from one source, and a fresh login followed by privileged changes.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: Measuring a service sandbox with systemd-analyze security
md: Every directive can break something: `MemoryDenyWriteExecute` breaks JIT runtimes, `ProtectProc=invisible` can break tools that inspect other processes, `ProcSubset=pid` is, per the manual, not suitable for most non-trivial programs. Add directives one at a time on a test host and watch the journal for denials.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: Falco: turning the system call stream into alerts
md: Falco watches system calls. In April 2025 the security company ARMO showed a proof-of-concept rootkit that does its file and network work through io_uring (lesson 6), and reported Falco's default rules did not see it. Lesson 13 covers what that means for every syscall-based sensor.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: Patching a fleet: automatic updates, restarts, reboots and rings
md: "Installed" is the most common false comfort in patch reports. The xz-utils and regreSSHion fixes did nothing for a daemon that kept running the old code; libraries need service restarts and kernels need reboots or livepatches. Report on what is running.

courseTitle: LLM-as-judge for relevance labeling
lessonTitle: From labels to leaderboards: do system rankings survive?
md: Label-level agreement can be modest (kappa 0.3 to 0.6) while system-level agreement is high (tau near 0.9), because errors that are not systematic average out over many queries. The reverse also holds: a small systematic bias can flip close systems even when kappa looks fine.

courseTitle: Evaluating generated text: metrics, LLM judges and human preference
lessonTitle: Task-specific eval sets, regression tests and significance
md: Report a gain as an interval, computed by resampling items with both systems paired. If the interval includes zero, say "not distinguishable on this set" and either add items or keep the old version. Check slices as well as the average.

courseTitle: LLM inference systems and KV-cache memory management
lessonTitle: Measuring a server: latency percentiles, load curves and benchmarks
md: A serving benchmark is a curve, not a number: sweep the request rate with random arrivals, and at each rate report p50 and p99 of TTFT, TPOT and ITL plus goodput under your SLOs. Throughput equals offered load until saturation, so the interesting part is where latency bends.

courseTitle: LLM inference systems and KV-cache memory management
lessonTitle: Who goes next: priority, fairness and length-aware scheduling
md: Admission decides whether a request fits; ordering decides who waits. FCFS is simple but lets long jobs block short ones. SJF by predicted rank cuts mean latency, VTC shares service fairly between clients, and explicit priorities protect interactive traffic, each with a guard against starvation.

courseTitle: LLM prompting and structured output: from prompts to masked logits
lessonTitle: Validation, retries and the pitfalls of strict formats
md: Treat structured output as a contract with three checks: did it finish (stop reason), does it fit (schema, often enforced by the decoder), and is it right (your validators and evals, test sets of inputs with known good answers). Leave the model an honest way out, put reasoning before answers, and measure quality with and without the constraint.

courseTitle: Latency and cost tradeoffs for LLM reranking
lessonTitle: Anatomy of one rerank call: tokens in, tokens out, two phases
md: Misconception: "output is only 60 tokens, so it is negligible." For billing it is small. For latency it is not, because prefill reads thousands of tokens in parallel while decode produces tokens one step at a time.

courseTitle: LLM as reranker: pointwise, pairwise and listwise prompting
lessonTitle: Why use an LLM as the last-stage reranker
md: An LLM reranker is a prompt plus an aggregation rule. Pointwise, pairwise and listwise differ in what one call sees (1, 2 or a window of passages) and therefore in how many calls a ranking needs and how hard each call is.

courseTitle: LLM routing and cascades: cheap model or strong model
lessonTitle: Managed routing in Amazon Bedrock, and how routers fail
md: Routing failures are silent. A wrong answer from the weak model looks like any other answer, and the dashboard shows only that costs went down. Log the routed model with every response (Bedrock returns it), and compare quality by route, not just overall.

courseTitle: Local feature matching: Harris, SIFT, ORB and RANSAC
